activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow squeaks underfoot when it is very cold, because the hard ice crystals rub and break instead of melting slightly under pressure.
story:
Ryder had waited all morning for the snow to stop, and by ten o'clock it finally did, so he pulled on his boots and ran to the park two blocks away, where Crosby was already packing a snow fort beside the climbing structure. Every step Ryder took made a strange squeaking crunch, like a rubber duck being stepped on, and when he reached Crosby he turned around and walked a small circle just to hear it again.

"It does that when it's freezing out," Crosby said, stomping his own boot. "Really cold snow squeaks because the hard ice crystals rub and break instead of melting a little under your weight." Ryder frowned. Yesterday the snow had gone almost silent, and it had been warmer, but he wasn't sure he believed that one warm day proved anything. He wanted to verify it himself, with a fair test.

So they tried walking in different spots. The snow near the playground equipment, where kids had trampled it into a hard crust, squeaked sharply. Out by the fence, where the snow lay fluffy and soft, their boots went in with more of a hollow crunch and less of a squeak. Ryder crouched and pressed his mitten flat against the packed patch, then the fluffy patch, feeling the difference in how each one gave way. "So packed snow means it was handled more, and the cold makes the crystals squeaky when they break," he said slowly, working it out. "Then anything nobody touched should squeak too."

They stamped a clean rectangle of untouched snow by the pond, and it squeaked loud enough that a woman walking her dog looked over and laughed. At the shelter by the ball diamond, Ms. Zhu was scraping ice off the water fountain with her mitten, and she asked what they were doing. "Science," Crosby said. "Snow squeaks when it's very cold." She told them an anecdote about her brother measuring the squeak one winter with a thermometer and swearing the coldest days were the squeakiest, which made Ryder grin, because his own test had just agreed with hers.

By the time they headed home, the sun had come out but the air was still bitter, and their footsteps squeaked the whole way. Ryder decided no fair test could make him immune to the fun of it, and he walked twice around the park gate just to hear the sound one more time before Crosby shouted, "Race you to the sidewalk!"

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In Canada, a federal bill must pass three readings in both the House of Commons and the Senate before it can receive royal assent.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like burnt toast and maple syrup, which was normal for a Saturday, but Jaxson barely noticed. He had his mom's old laptop open on the table, squinting at a website about a bill that might, someday, make school lunches free across Canada. He wanted to write a whole report about it for Monday, and he wanted to be the kid who actually knew what he was talking about.

"Six," he muttered, drawing on a napkin. "Three readings in the House of Commons, then three more in the Senate. That's six stops." He tapped the screen. "It's passed two so far. So Khadijah owes me a dollar."

His grandpa slid a plate of toast toward him. "Why does she owe you a dollar?"

"She bet the bill was basically a law already. But it's only got royal assent after all six. She counted the readings like they were one big thing." Jaxson grinned. "She added wrong, which is beautiful, because she's the math kid."

Grandpa's landlord knocked on the back door right then, complaining about the gutter again, and Jaxson had to carry his napkin diagram to the living room to protect it. There he summarized the whole thing out loud to Josephine on a video call. "So a bill has to pass three readings in the House of Commons, and then three readings in the Senate. Only then does it get royal assent. Boom. Coherent. Monday, solved."

"That's the least coherent boom I've ever heard," Josephine said. "But okay. What if it fails a reading?"

Jaxson paused. He hadn't tested that. He scrolled, found the answer, and let out a groan. "Then it dies. Khadijah is going to be insufferable."

"So make the report a timeline," Josephine said. "Draw six little doors and a crown at the end."

Jaxson grabbed a marker and started drawing the first door, toast crumbs and all.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
Emile sat cross-legged on Angel's bedroom floor, holding Angel's phone while Angel dug through the closet for the good controller. On the screen, the group chat with Maddison blinked awake with a new message, all capital letters: WHERE ARE YOU GUYS. Emile read it twice. It looked angry, like a principal calling someone to the office.

Before he could answer, Maddison replied: why are you yelling?? Angel leaned over his shoulder, still holding a controller in each hand. "I wasn't yelling," Angel said, frowning at his own message. "I just wanted it to stand out so you'd actually see it." Maddison typed back a row of tiny laughing faces, which somehow made it worse. "So caps is like shouting on here," Emile said slowly, "even when nobody's mad." He had an idea, and since the phone was already in his hand, he tested it. He typed a reply in ordinary lowercase letters, all friendly: we're at angel's, working on the tower. come over if you want.

Maddison's answer came fast: ok that's better. you sounded so mad before lol. Angel flopped onto the bed, staring at the ceiling like it was personally unfair. "How was I supposed to know? Nobody handed me a rulebook."

"There kind of is one," Emile said. He opened a private message to Maddison, just her, not the whole group, and typed: angel didn't mean to sound mad. he says sorry. in the group it looked like a big deal but it was nothing. In the private chat it felt different, quieter, the way whispering in a hallway is different from announcing something to the whole cafeteria. Maddison replied with a thumbs up and then, a moment later: tell him to advocate for himself next time instead of making me guess.

They rebuilt the tower in the game until it stood perpendicular to the wall of Angel's desk, perfectly straight, and Emile thought about consequences, how one row of capital letters had almost cost them a whole afternoon. When Maddison knocked on the door twenty minutes later, she held up her phone. On the screen was a single message in enormous capitals: I'M HERE. "That one," she said, "is actual yelling."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts, while deodorants do not stop sweat but reduce or cover the smell.
story:
Sadie marched into the pharmacy like she was on a mission, because she was. In her backpack sat the evidence: a gym shirt with two gray circles under the arms, held up that morning by Bryden during math while the whole back row laughed. Her ambition was simple and enormous. She would never be embarrassed in gym class again.

"Deodorant aisle," she announced to Makena, who had tagged along for the walk home but now looked fully invested. "There has to be a whole wall of it."

There was. Blue cans, purple sticks, ones that claimed to be for men and ones covered in flowers. Sadie picked up the first stick and read the label, because her mother always said the answer was on the label if you stood there long enough. The word DEODORANT ran across the front. She flipped it over and scanned the back, frowning.

"It says it covers smell," she said. "It doesn't say anything about sweat." She grabbed the next one, a green stick with a glacier on it. This one said ANTIPERSPIRANT. The back panel said it reduced sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts. "So they're different things," she said slowly, holding both up like a game show host. "This one stops the wet. That one stops the smell."

"Then get the glacier one," Makena said. "Obviously."

"But wait." Sadie's brain was doing that thing where pieces clicked together. She thought about the kids in gym, about how some of them smelled fine but still had sweaty shirts, and others had dry shirts that smelled like old sandwiches. Two different problems. Two different products. It was a hidden rule, like figuring out which vending machine ate quarters. She tested her idea on a third label, a purple can: deodorant, nothing about sweat. A fourth: antiperspirant, nothing about covering smell. The pattern held.

"We need the one that does both," she declared, and found a stick that said ANTIPERSPIRANT DEODORANT on the front. She felt heat radiate from her face, but this time it was excitement, not embarrassment. She paid the cashier with crumpled bills and walked out holding the bag like a trophy.

At school the next morning, Sadie found Bryden at his locker and held up the bag. "Good news," she said. "I did research."

He went pale. "What research?"

She pulled out the shirt, which she had washed, dried, ironed, and, in a moment of pure eccentric genius, folded around the same green stick with a note taped on it: For you. Two problems, two fixes. Ask me how I know.

Bryden looked at the note, then at her, then whispered, "Does it work on nerves too? I have band solo Friday."

"Get in line," Sadie said. "I have gym at two."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: On Buddhist observance days called uposatha, devout lay Buddhists may take eight precepts, including not eating after midday.
story:
Eleanor had been looking forward to the food stalls at the cultural festival all week, so when her mother steered her toward the temple open house instead, she dragged her sneakers on the pavement. Inside, the hall smelled of incense and something like flower water. A woman with a clipboard handed Eleanor's mother a paper, and Eleanor saw the words "uposatha day" printed at the top.

"Uposatha," her mother said quietly, nodding at the paper. "That's why the kitchen is closed until tomorrow."

Eleanor scanned the schedule anyway, because she didn't believe her stomach, which was already growling, should have to wait. It was barely one o'clock. Then she noticed the pattern herself: everyone with a sticker on their shirt had eaten before noon, and the long table of rice and curries had been cleared at midday, not one plate left. She counted the rules on the paper her mother held. Eight precepts, and one of them, marked with a small star, was not eating after midday.

Taya from her class waved from near the altar, holding a paper cup of tea. "Come sit with us," Taya said. "My grandma does the eight precepts every uposatha. I ate a big lunch at eleven thirty, so I'm fine." Eleanor sat down between Taya and an old man who was folding paper lotuses, his fingers quick and sure. He showed Eleanor how to fold one, and she petitioned him with her eyes until he laughed and gave her a square of gold paper.

She had been biased against the whole afternoon, deciding it would be boring without snacks, but the folding took all her attention. Her lotus came out lopsided. The old man set it on the altar beside a bronze vessel filled with water, next to his own, and pressed his palms together. Eleanor copied him, not sure she was doing it right. Her stomach growled again, loudly, and Taya snorted.

"It's okay," Taya whispered. "My stomach did that at two o'clock last time. Grandma says the hunger passes, like a wave."

Eleanor watched the worshippers, some kneeling, some chatting softly, and thought about how she'd figured out the no-eating rule from the empty tables before anyone told her. It felt like solving a puzzle where the answer had been hiding in plain sight. When her mother touched her shoulder near sunset, Eleanor stood slowly and looked back at the altar, at her crooked lotus floating in the lamplight.

"Can we come back next month?" she asked. "I want to fold a better one. And I'll eat a bigger lunch at eleven thirty."

Taya held up her hand for a high five.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: The Northeast blackout that began on August 14, 2003, cut power to about 55 million people in parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada.
story:
Aiden was halfway through a frozen pizza when every light on the street died at once. The oven ticked into silence, the fridge stopped humming, and the house went so dark he could see the outline of his own hand only when he waved it in front of his face. He fumbled for the flashlight in the kitchen drawer, found a dead one, then a second one that worked, and carried it out to the porch, where his neighbours Camelia and Margo were already sitting on their steps.

"It's the whole street," Camelia said, pointing her phone screen down the road. Every porch light was out, and the streetlamps stood dark and symmetrical, spaced like the teeth of a very tired comb.

"Come over here," called Mr. Toussaint from next door, holding up a lantern. "Power cuts are better with company and lemonade." The lemonade was warm, but nobody complained. Aiden told him about the pizza, and how his mom had gone out to buy a replacement before it could germinate into a full science experiment, and everyone laughed.

"Biggest one I ever saw was August 14, 2003," Mr. Toussaint said, settling into his chair. "A blackout that day cut power to about 55 million people, in parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada. I walked home from work, whole city pouring out of the buildings. Took me four hours. A man sold warm water bottles on a corner like it was treasure."

Aiden turned the flashlight over in his hands, thinking. Fifty-five million people. That was a blackout that spread across a whole region, like ink in water. He looked down the street again. Four blocks away, he could see a glow, faint but definitely there. He stood up. "If this were huge, everything would be dark, right? But it's not. My diagnosis: something took out just our loop." He traced the street with the flashlight beam. "So it's probably a branch on a line, or a transformer, somewhere close."

Margo grabbed her shoes. They walked two blocks, following the boundary between dark and lit houses like a seam, until they found it: a maple limb lying across the sagging power line at the end of Almond Street, its leaves still trembling.

"There," Aiden said. "Fifty-five million people had to walk home in that one. We just have to walk to the end of the block." Camelia was already dialing the power company, and Margo held up her phone and snapped a picture of the branch, saying, "For the pizza's memorial."

activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
knowledge_domain: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
fact: The eastern half of the Roman Empire, later called the Byzantine Empire, lasted almost a thousand years longer, until the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople in 1453.
story:
Rose pressed her finger on the museum map until the plexiglass squeaked. The Roman Empire spread across the wall in two colours, red in the west and purple in the east, split by a diagonal line that cut through the middle like someone had taken scissors to the world.

"It fell in 476," said Genesis, who had read exactly one plaque and now considered herself an expert. "It says so right there."

"Then why is there purple still on the map after that?" Rose traced the eastern border with her eyes, down through Greece, up around the Black Sea, all the way to a city marked Constantinople. Something about the shape bothered her, the way the purple part went on and on while the red part just stopped.

Jaycee leaned in. "Maybe the map is wrong."

"Maps in museums aren't wrong," Rose said. "They're just not finished being read."

She remembered Ms. Yamamoto's classroom three weeks earlier, the day of the timeline disaster. Ms. Yamamoto had unrolled a long paper strip across the floor and asked them to place cards with dates on it. Rose had squinted at the card that said 1453 and assumed it was a misprint, because everyone knew Rome fell way back around 476, and there was a gap the size of an ocean between them. She had even written "typo?" on it in pencil. Ms. Yamamoto had looked at the pencil mark, then at Rose, and said only, "Cards can go more than one place on a timeline." Rose had gone home and erased the pencil.

She found the exhibit booklet and flipped past the coins and the mosaics until she reached a page headed with a date: 1453. Ottoman Turks, it said. Constantinople. Captured. She read it twice, then three times, her finger moving along each line.

"Genesis. Come here."

"What."

"Read this."

Genesis read. Her face did the thing faces do when a fact arrives that a person had not ordered. "So Rome fell twice?"

"No." Rose pointed back at the big map, at the purple half, at the line of the border that had held for centuries after the red half was gone. "The eastern half lasted longer. Almost a thousand years longer. It got called the Byzantine Empire, and it came to its end right here, in 1453, when the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople." She tapped the city. "It fell there. The west fell earlier. Two different falls, one empire that split."

Jaycee looked at the map, then at Rose, then at the map again. "So when you said maps aren't finished being read."

"I interpret, therefore I win the argument," Rose said.

Genesis took out her phone to photograph the plaque that said 476, then, with visible despair, photographed the booklet page too. Rose slid her museum pencil along the diagonal border, purple edge to the Black Sea, and said, "Same pencil, by the way. Never borrow my pencil."

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: Python uses indentation to show which lines belong inside a loop; a line that is not indented runs only once, after the loop has finished.
story:
Abigail typed her name into the login screen and watched the computer lab's old machines groan to life. Mr. Wijaya had written the assignment on the board: write a Python loop that asks the user for a number and prints the whole times table for it. Easy, Abigail thought. She had already written half the program in her notebook during lunch, right after the part where she'd helped Simone install a game on Simone's laptop, which had taken three tries and one very vague error message.

She typed the program carefully. "Which number?" the screen asked. She typed 7. Then she waited. And waited. The cursor blinked. Then a single line appeared: 7 times 12 is 84. Nothing else. Twelve rows should have printed, one for each number from 1 to 12, and instead she had the last row and only the last row, sitting there alone like the final survivor of something terrible.

"That's all I got too," Adriel whispered from the next computer. His screen showed 9 times 12 is 108 and nothing before it. Simone leaned over from across the aisle. "Mine does the same thing. Only the last row. I think the computers are broken." Abigail almost agreed. The lab machines were ancient, half of them still had a drawing of a butterfly larva stuck on as somebody's old screensaver joke, and "the computers are broken" was a perfectly good excuse. She raised her hand anyway.

Mr. Wijaya came over, looked at her screen, and smiled in a way that told her nothing. "Count your lines," he said, and walked away. Count her lines. Abigail stared at the program. The print statement that showed the answer sat at the left edge of the screen, lined up exactly with the word for. The line above it, the one that moved the number forward, started four spaces in. She counted again. Four spaces. Then zero. She remembered Mr. Wijaya saying it once, back in September, and she'd thought it was a small thing: "Python uses indentation to show which lines belong inside a loop." She had assumed the spaces were just decoration, like paragraph margins in an essay.

Her hand hovered over the spacebar. If the spaces were the rule, then the print line, the one with no spaces, wasn't inside the loop at all. It would run only once, after the loop had finished, after the counting had already gone all the way to 12. Which would mean the computer hadn't lost the first eleven rows. It had never printed them. She pressed the spacebar four times, ran the program, and typed 7. Row after row spilled down the screen, 7 times 1 is 7, 7 times 2 is 14, all the way to 84. "Spaces," she said to Adriel. "It was the spaces the whole time."

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: In a chemical change, atoms rearrange to make one or more new substances with different properties from what you started with.
story:
The toaster popped and the kitchen smelled like a small campfire. Isabelle pried out the toast, black and stiff, and set it on a plate next to two slices that had stayed golden. On the counter waited her science homework: "Give one example of a physical change and one of a chemical change from your own kitchen." The problem was that she wasn't sure which one burnt toast was, and Kimberly had texted her an hour ago insisting it was still bread, just brown, the way ice was still water. "No way," Isabelle had typed back. Then she had stared at the phone, because honestly, she wasn't sure.

She tried the golden toast first. She bent it, crumbled a corner, and even dropped it in a glass of water, where it went soggy and swelled like a tiny white tsunami rising over the rim. Annoying, but interesting. Soft bread, soggy bread, crumbled bread: still bread, she decided. Nothing new had shown up. That felt like the melting kind of change, the kind her textbook called physical, temporary, like ice going back to water.

The burnt slice was different. She scraped the black part with a knife and got a flaky powder that smelled like nothing she could name, certainly not bread. She licked a crumb of the golden toast, then a speck of the black powder, and made a face. Bitter, smoky, wrong. She thought about her grandmother's old bike in the garage, its fender orange with rust that had definitely not been there when the bike was new. The metal hadn't just gotten wet and dried; something else had formed on it, something that hadn't existed before.

That was the piece she'd been missing. "In a chemical change, atoms rearrange to make one or more new substances with different properties," she said out loud to the empty kitchen, testing the sentence like a recipe. Atoms. Rearrange. New substances. She looked at the powder on her knife. Could burnt toast be a new substance with different properties? It tasted different, smelled different, flaked instead of bending. Bread couldn't do that. She felt the idea click into place, the same click as when she'd finally understood why her mother donated blood: something leaves one thing and becomes part of another.

She texted Kimberly: "Come over. Bring your nose." When Kimberly arrived, Isabelle lined up three plates: golden toast, soggy toast, and the black powder. "Bend the first one," she said. Kimberly bent it. "Now try to bend the burnt one." Kimberly pressed down; it snapped and crumbled into flakes that skittered across the plate. Kimberly sniffed it and pulled back. "Okay," she said slowly. "That is not bread." Isabelle grinned and slid the science notebook across the table, already open to a blank page. "So help me figure out if scrambled eggs count too."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Saying 'I'm sorry if you were upset' is often called a non-apology, because it expresses regret about the other person's feelings rather than about what the speaker did.
story:
Layla pushed the folded note across the lab table toward Zachariah and waited while he read it. "I'm sorry if you got upset at lunch," he read out loud. "Wait. If I got upset?" He set the note down between the beakers. "That makes it sound like it's my fault for being upset. Like I overreacted."

"It was for Nadia," Layla said. "We haven't talked since Tuesday." Nadia had told Layla that her science fair project was copied from a website, and Layla had said something sharp about Nadia's art poster being traced. Both of them had been wrong, but only one of them had written a note.

Zachariah turned the paper over, studying it like it was data. "You know what my sister calls that? A non-apology. It says sorry about the other person's feelings, not about what you actually did." He tapped the word "if." "That little word is doing all the work. Take it out and see what's left."

Layla covered the note with her hand. She had spent all of Thursday drafting it, and now she could see the flaw plainly, the way you suddenly see the pattern in a math problem. "If I only apologize for her feelings, I'm not apologizing for what I said." The insight felt significant, but it also stung. She had been so careful with the wording, and the wording was exactly the problem.

At lunch she found Nadia alone at the far table. "Can I petition for a redo?" Layla asked, sliding into the seat across from her. "I wrote you a note, but Zachariah read it and it was a non-apology. I'm not sorry you got upset. I'm sorry I said your poster was traced. That was mean, and I said it because I was embarrassed about my project."

Nadia looked at her for a long moment, then pulled the traced-and-painted poster from her bag and unrolled it on the table. "Sit closer," she said. "I'll show you the part I'm actually proud of."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Hatching shades an area with rows of parallel lines, and cross-hatching adds another set of lines crossing them to make the area darker.
story:
The art shed at Camp Wren had exactly one good lamp, and Mia claimed it before anyone else could. She set her paper on the table, clipped it down, and stared at the task Mr. Han had written on the board: draw a sphere with a light source, showing highlight, shadow, and cast shadow. Pencils only, he had said, because pencil can smudge from light to dark. But when Mia opened her pencil case, she found three rebellious pens that had shoved their way past the pencils she thought she'd packed, and not one soft gray stick among them. The pencil sharpener on the shelf was empty too. All she had were lines.

She tested the idea the only way she could. In the corner of the page she drew a small patch of short parallel lines, all leaning the same way, evenly spaced. From a distance it looked like a pale gray wash. That was something. She drew another patch, this time laying a second set of lines across the first, crossing them at an angle, and the patch went darker, dark enough that it read as shadow. She sat back, pleased and a little surprised. Pure black ink, and somehow she had gray.

Elliot dropped onto the bench across from her, holding a half-finished sketch of the lake. He wanted his drawing in the display case by the dining hall before the parents' visit on Friday, and he kept counting the days out loud. "Two more mornings," he said. "What are you doing with all those stripes?"

"It's called hatching," Mia said, turning her page so he could see the corner patch. "And when you cross the lines, it's cross-hatching. Watch." She laid a third set over the second patch and it darkened again, like dusk coming on in stages.

She formulated a plan as she worked: hatching for the sphere's lit side, where the lines could stay thin and far apart, cross-hatching near the bottom curve where the light gave up, and the cast shadow under the sphere darker than anything, since it was the light being blocked completely. For the highlight she would leave a small circle of bare paper, untouched ink-white. Tamara leaned over from the next table and squinted at the drawing. "It looks round," she said, "and it's nothing but lines. That's weird."

Mr. Han walked the rows slowly, hands behind his back. He stopped at Mia's page and tilted his head, and the lamplight fell across the sphere so that the real shadow of her pen lay across her drawn one. "Nice mechanism," he said quietly, tapping the corner where her test patches were. Mia picked the pen back up and began the cast shadow, line over line over line.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Squeezing or popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin and can leave scars.
story:
Clara sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table and pressed two fingers against the small red bump on her chin. Her thumb and forefinger opposed each other, ready to squeeze, because Amira's birthday party was Saturday and she was not going to a party with a pimple. She was ten minutes early for her checkup, alone in the room, and nobody would ever know.

Her phone buzzed. A text from Amira: "DON'T pop it. My sister says squeezing pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin and it can leave scars. She has a scar. It's real. Just wash it and leave it alone." Clara stared at the message, then at the mirror on the cabinet door. A scar, forever, versus a red bump for three days. She lowered her fingers. It felt like the worst trade in history, but she made it.

The door opened and Ms. Çelik, the nurse, came in with a clipboard. She looked at Clara's chin, then at Clara's face. "Ah, the first one," she said kindly. "Your mom mentioned puberty runs early in your family heritage. Grandmothers, mothers, daughters." Clara slumped. "So it's going to keep happening? And I smell like a gym sock even when I haven't done anything?" Ms. Çelik laughed. "Sweat glands wake up around now. Daily shower, deodorant every morning, and wash your face. That's the whole battle plan." She pointed at the barren white wall where a poster showed a kid the same age as Clara, arrows pointing to armpits and a smiling face. "Hormones," the poster said, like that explained everything.

On Saturday, Clara stood in front of Amira's mirror wearing the new deodorant she had bought with her own money. The bump was smaller. Not gone, but smaller, and no scar, and no gym-sock smell. Callum was already in the kitchen yelling about cake. Clara straightened her party hat and walked out to join him.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
Antoine stared at his phone in Ms. Tan's classroom after school, waiting for his mom, and typed into the group chat: "Tournament is Saturday. We need a fourth player. Asiya, Vihaan, vote." The basketball tournament allowed only one sub besides the starters, and three names had already come up: Vihaan himself, a kid named Ravi from another class, and Antoine's cousin. The chat filled fast. Vihaan sent, "Ravi and your cousin both average 10 points a game. Same number. So it doesn't matter, pick either." Antoine started to agree, then paused. He had watched both of them play at the park on Saturdays, and they did not feel the same at all.

"Hold on," he typed. "Send me the points from every game, not just the average." Vihaan sent a photo of the rec center's stat sheet, which somebody's older brother had photographed off the corkboard next to the polymer-science-fair posters. Antoine read down the columns twice. His cousin had scored 10, 10, 9, 11, 10. Ravi had scored 24, 0, 20, 1, 5. Antoine counted each column three times, because the totals looked wrong. They weren't. Both added up to 50 points over five games.

"Whoa," he typed. "Same average. But look at Ravi's games. He either goes off or disappears." Asiya replied with a row of laughing faces, then, "So who's better?" Antoine's thumbs hovered. It would be naive to just take the average and call it settled, he thought, because the average hid the thing that actually mattered: one player showed up every game, and one swung between great and terrible. "My cousin," he typed. "He gives us 10 points every single game. Ravi might give us 24. Or he might give us zero, and we lose by two." Vihaan asked him to elaborate, so Antoine sent the five numbers for each player, one after another, like a bar graph made of texts.

There was a long pause, then Asiya sent, "Okay. Steady beats streaky when you only get one shot. Voting cousin." Vihaan sent a single word: "Fine." Then he added, "You're still running the point though, because if I average four turnovers a game, nobody's checking the spread on that." Antoine laughed out loud in the empty classroom, and Ms. Tan looked up from her desk and asked what was so funny. He held up his phone so she could see the stream of numbers. "Saturday's roster," he said. "Official."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches the eyes and makes them water.
story:
Beatrice stood at her grandmother's counter with three onions and her grandmother's biggest knife, and she was determined to make the soup by herself. Grandma was resting upstairs, and the recipe card in her looping handwriting said French onion soup, the one Grandpa always asked for. Beatrice had promised it for his birthday dinner, and tonight was the night.

The first onion was easy. She peeled it, cut it in half, and then sliced through it, and within seconds her eyes were burning and streaming. She blinked, wiped her face on her sleeve, and kept chopping, but by the second onion she could barely see the cutting board. "How can a vegetable do this to a person?" she muttered, sniffing.

Brodie had asked the exact same question last autumn, she remembered, when the two of them had helped his mother chop onions for chili. He had stood at the sink crying his eyes out and insisting something in his own life must be upsetting him, some hidden sadness, because surely a vegetable couldn't make you weep. His mother had just laughed and handed him a paper towel. Beatrice had laughed too, at the time, though now she wondered whether she should have. She had told him it was only an illusion, that his tears meant nothing. That had been wrong, in a way she couldn't quite name yet.

She set down the knife and thought about it. Something had to travel from the onion to her eyes, because her eyes weren't touching anything. That meant the onion was releasing something into the air when she cut it, and the only moment it started was the moment the knife went through. So the whole thing was her own doing, in a sense. She tested it: she set one whole, uncut onion on the counter and stared at it for a full minute. Nothing. Her eyes stayed dry. Then she made one slice in it, and within ten seconds the stinging started again. Whatever it was, the cutting released it.

So she adjusted her plan. She moved the cutting board to the sink, turned the cold tap on low, and chopped with the water running between her and the onions, keeping her face turned away as she worked. It wasn't perfect, but the tears slowed enough for her to finish all three onions and get them sizzling in the buttered pot, filling the kitchen with the smell that meant the soup was really underway.

When Grandpa came in from the garden, he found her at the stove with red-rimmed eyes and a triumphant grin. "Been crying over me, Bea?" he asked.

"Onions," she said, and slid the wooden spoon toward him for a taste. "But I figured out how to fight back."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
Florence typed her name into the sign-up page for the third time, and for the third time a red message appeared at the top of the screen. You must be 13 or older to create an account. She was eleven, and the number would not change no matter how many times she refreshed the page. The whole class was on the app already, sharing drawings and jokes, and she wanted in before Monday.

She pulled up a video call, and Anaelle's face appeared in a small square on the screen. "It asked me my birthday and then it just stopped," Florence said. "Like it's checking."

Anaelle held up her phone so Florence could see her older brother, who was flipping through a search page. "It's a law," he said, reading. "The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998. It says websites need parental consent before they collect personal information from anyone under thirteen."

"So that's why they all ask your birthday," Anaelle said. "They have to know how old you are before they can take your name and stuff."

Florence sat back. So the app wasn't being mean on purpose. It was being careful, because collecting her name, her birthday, her drawings, would count as collecting personal information from someone under thirteen. "Wait," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "If my mom consents, would that work?"

She scrolled to the bottom of the sign-up page and found a small grey link she had skipped before: Options for users under 13. Behind it was a permission form, with a space for a parent's email. She called her mom over to the desk. Her mom read the whole form, every line, while Florence waited with her hands folded.

"Some of this really could invade your privacy, you know," her mom said, pointing at a part about location data. "But there's a setting here to turn that off." She clicked it herself, then typed her email and pressed send.

"Can I tell Ms. Goh about the form?" Florence asked. "Azaan couldn't sign up either. He thought he'd been banned."

"Tell him it was the law, not him," her mom said.

Florence messaged Azaan right away: it's not a ban, there's a permission form, I'll send you the link. He replied with a thumbs-up, then a drawing of a judge holding a gavel, with FLORENCE written underneath in block letters. She laughed and set it as her first post.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Each degree of latitude or longitude is divided into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds, to pinpoint an exact spot.
story:
Naomi spread the old map across her grandmother's dining room table, weighting the curling corners with salt shakers. Grandpa had left a note in his desk before he passed: "The good pen is at 40 degrees, 44 minutes north, 73 degrees, 59 minutes west. You'll know how to find it." The pen was the silver one he'd used to sign every birthday card, and Naomi wanted it more than anything in the house.

Her friend Anaelle leaned over the map, frowning. "Minutes? Like, at 12:44? Do we have to go somewhere at a certain time?" That was exactly what Naomi had assumed at first, but it nagged at her. Her grandfather had written those numbers as a location, not a time. She traced her finger along the faint lines running across the map and noticed tiny marks between the numbered ones. There were sixty of them, she counted, tucked between 40 degrees and 41 degrees. Sixty again between the next pair. The same pattern showed on the lines running the other way.

"So it's not time at all," Naomi said slowly. "The degrees are cut into sixty parts, and they call those parts minutes." She checked the second coordinate the same way, counting along the vertical lines. Sure enough, each degree of longitude broke into sixty minutes too, and when she squinted, each minute had its own tiny subdivisions. "Look. Each minute divides into sixty seconds. It's like a clock, but it's measuring the Earth, not the day."

They had a new problem, though. The seconds weren't written on the note, and the dining room clock's ticking had begun to make Naomi nervous, as if the map itself might cease to exist before they finished. "We only have degrees and minutes," Anaelle said. "That gives us a whole rectangle of city, not one spot." Naomi refused to panic. She marked the rectangle, then pulled out her phone and typed the coordinates in, adding zeroes for seconds. A dot appeared on a bridge in the park, right where her grandfather used to stop and watch the rowboats.

The park was ten minutes away by bike, real minutes, and the two of them rode fast. Under the third bench on the bridge, taped where only someone looking would find it, lay a small velvet box. Inside was the silver pen and a folded card in her grandfather's looping, eloquent handwriting: "Now write back." Naomi laughed out loud, and Anaelle grabbed her arm. "Write back where?"

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
story:
Juliette sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field, her right arm propped in a blue sling, watching Kingston and Justice run drills without her. Two weeks ago she had fallen off the monkey bars, and now her broken arm lived inside a hard white cast that itched in the afternoons. In her left hand she held the X-ray printout the doctor had given her, because she had asked to keep it, and because she could not stop staring at it.

"Are you looking at your arm again?" Justice asked, jogging over at the water break, sweat sticking her hair to her forehead.

"Look." Juliette held up the film. "My bones are white. Really white, like chalk. But my skin and my muscles, you can barely see them. Why would a picture show one part of me and not the rest? It's all me."

Kingston leaned in, breathing hard. "Maybe the machine only likes bones."

Juliette gave him a look of gentle skepticism, one eyebrow up. "Machines don't like things, Kingston. But something is different about bones. Something that doesn't coincide with the rest of the body." She tapped the film with her good hand. "What do bones have that muscles don't?"

Justice frowned. "They're hard?"

"Hard how, though?" Juliette had been chewing on this all week. She remembered the milk ads at school, the ones about strong bones. "Milk. My mom is always on me about milk. Milk has calcium, and calcium makes bones hard." She paused, turning the idea over like a stone in her pocket. "Maybe the calcium is why they show up white. Maybe the calcium soaks up the X-rays, more than the soft stuff around it, so bones come out bright and skin almost vanishes."

"So drink more milk, get whiter bones?" Kingston said.

"No, you'd get stronger bones. The white part is just how the picture turns out." Juliette looked around the field, then down at her cast. "I want to test it."

"Test it how?" Justice asked. "You can't X-ray yourself."

Juliette stood up, tucked the film under her sling, and marched across the grass toward Mr. Francis, who was coaching the younger kids' team on the far end. He was a vigorous walker even standing still, always clapping, always moving. She waited for the whistle, then asked him whether the school nurse kept anything from when students got hurt.

"The nurse has an old light board for looking at X-rays," he said. "Why?"

Juliette explained, pointing at her film, at the glowing bones and the ghost of her arm around them. Mr. Francis nodded along but offered no explanation, only said, "Sounds like you've got a theory. Nurse's office closes at four."

So that was where they went, all three of them, the film clipped to the light board, the white bones blazing against the dim gray of everything else. Juliette held up her hand next to it, her real hand, ordinary and invisible to X-rays in all the ways that mattered, and grinned.

"Calcium," she said. "My bones are full of it, and they drink up the picture."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: A theme is usually written about people in general rather than one character, so it could apply to readers' lives outside the book.
story:
The assignment sheet said "Theme: a statement about life, supported by a quotation," which was easy to print and impossible to fill in. Juliette sat at the corner table in the school library with her copy of the novel open, a pencil, and a legal pad that still showed the ghost of her last attempt, erased so hard it had a hole in it. Her first try had been "Auggie learns to be brave." Mr. Bekele had looked at it during yesterday's class, made a small sound like a kettle deciding not to boil, and written "closer" in green pen. Closer. Not even close. Closer.

"You've been staring at that page for ten minutes," said Alexandra, sliding into the chair across from her. Elliot arrived next, carrying two cookies and no visible intention of sharing either.

"Auggie learns to be brave," Juliette said. "That's what the book is about."

"That's what the book is about for Auggie," Alexandra said.

Juliette was about to argue when she flashed back to September, when she'd spent a whole weekend building a model bridge for science that had collapsed under one textbook. Her father had said the problem wasn't the popsicle sticks, it was that she'd calibrated the load for one book instead of a shelf of them. She hadn't known what calibrated meant then, so she'd looked it up, which was the only part of the weekend she enjoyed.

She looked down at "Auggie learns to be brave." It held up for one character. A shelf would hold more.

"What if I take his name out?" she said slowly. "People learn to be brave even when it's hard to be seen. Something like that."

Elliot stopped chewing. "That's about, like, everyone. That's about me. I'm learning to raise my hand in math."

"Then it's a theme," Alexandra said. "A theme is usually written about people in general rather than one character, so it could apply to your actual life outside the book." She said it the way she said everything, as though it had been obvious since kindergarten.

"That's why he wrote 'closer,'" Juliette said. "My sentence only worked for Auggie. A theme has to work for a shelf of people." Now she needed a quotation. She flipped pages, hunting for the scene where Auggie stands in front of the class on the first day, and found the line where he thinks that if they're going to stare, he'll give them something worth staring at. She copied it out, then tested it against her sentence. It fit. It even fit Elliot, who had once given a book report entirely facing the window.

The motive for her earlier failure was suddenly clear: she'd been writing a book report in disguise. Themes weren't about what happened to somebody. They were about what happens to everybody, a gradual kind of truth, the kind you don't notice arriving.

Mr. Bekele passed the table on his way to shelve a cart of returns. He glanced at her pad, and the kettle sound did not come.

"About time," he said. "Now find your quotation."

"Found it," Juliette said, and turned the pad so he could see.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fast growth during puberty often causes stretch marks, thin lines on the skin that are common and usually fade over time.
story:
The minivan smelled like sunscreen and warm vinyl, and Mathis was squished in the back between Lilianna and Nixon, all three of them buckled in for the twenty-minute drive to Mira's pool party. Lilianna kept her towel wrapped around her waist even though the heater was on.

"You okay back there?" the driver asked from the front. "Party starts at two, so we're on schedule."

"I'm fine," Lilianna said, but she pulled the towel tighter.

Mathis had noticed her hovering by the locker room mirror after gym all week, turning sideways, tugging her shirt down over her hips. He had a guess about why, and he decided to test it. "Lilianna. Is it lines? Like, thin lines on your skin?"

Her face went red. "How did you know?"

"Because I have them too." He pushed up his sleeve and showed the inside of his elbow, where a few pale thin lines ran beside the crease. "I grew two inches since June. The nurse at camp called them stretch marks. She said fast growing does that."

Lilianna leaned over and looked, still not touching the towel. "Really? On your arm?"

"On my knees too. Look." He pulled up his pant leg. "Nixon, check yours."

Nixon examined his own knees and shrugged. "Nothing. I haven't grown since third grade."

"That's why," Mathis said. He had worked out the pattern in his head: fast growth, then lines. Slow growth, no lines. "The nurse said they're common and they fade over time. My cousin had a bunch on his shoulders and now you can barely see them."

On the radio, the news was droning about a frog species threatened with extinction, and the driver turned it down. "Everything all right back there?"

"Fine," all three of them said at once.

Lilianna pulled the towel open a crack and looked down at her hips. "They're kind of transparent-looking. Like, thin. I thought something was wrong with me."

"They diminish," Nixon said, proud of the word. "That's what things do when they fade. My science teacher says it about sound."

"They fade," Mathis agreed. "Pool's in ten minutes. You going in the water or sitting on a chair all afternoon?"

Lilianna looked at the towel, then out the window at the first rooftops of Mira's neighborhood. She folded the towel into her bag and zipped it shut. "Race you to the deep end."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: A testimonial uses a famous or admired person to endorse something, even though that person may have no special knowledge about it and may be paid.
story:
The mall speakers hummed as Aiden pressed his nose to the sneaker store window. Behind the glass, a poster the size of a door showed Darius Cole, the best point guard in the league, holding up the Velocity X. "Everyone's wearing them," said Liliana beside him. "Half our grade already has a pair." Aiden had saved nine weeks of allowance, and the cumulative total in his pocket felt heavy. But something bothered him, and it bothered him like a splinter he couldn't reach.

He scrutinized the poster, corner to corner. In tiny gray letters at the bottom it said, "Darius Cole is compensated for this endorsement." He read it twice. "Compensated," he said slowly. "That means paid." Liliana leaned in and squinted like a laser beam had shot from her eyes to the fine print. "Wait. So Darius Cole gets money to hold these up? Does he even pick them himself?" That was exactly the question gnawing at Aiden. The poster made it look like Darius loved the shoes, but Darius was famous for basketball, not for knowing shoes. Being paid didn't prove he'd chosen them at all.

Inside, the shelves shouted words like "revolutionary," "unstoppable," and "legend." Aiden turned one box over. Same basic cushioning as the forty-dollar pair on the bottom shelf. He tried both on and walked the aisle, jumped twice, and ran a short lap past the cashier. His feet couldn't tell the difference. When Liliana texted her brother, his reply buzzed back a moment later: "Dear Aiden, I fell for a famous guy's ad once, spent eighty dollars on headphones he probably never touched. Save your money, or don't, but now you know how it works. Signed, Marco." Aiden laughed out loud in the middle of the store.

At the register, Ms. Dhillon, his neighbor, was buying socks. She raised an eyebrow at the forty-dollar box under his arm. "Smart choice," she said. Aiden grinned. "Famous people can sell anything," he told her. "Even stuff they know nothing about." He laced up the new shoes right there on the bench and stood up. "Watch this," he said, and sprinted a lap around the fountain.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: People with age-related hearing loss find it especially hard to follow speech when there is background noise.
story:
Grandpa had been staying with Luke's family for three days, and so far the week was going great. At the breakfast table they had talked about everything, baseball, the old house on Cedar Street, Grandpa's stories about being a paperboy. Grandpa caught every word, even when Luke mumbled. So on Saturday, Luke decided to take him to the Riverside Market, where Forrest and Emerson were helping Mr. Taylor run his vegetable stall.

The market roared. Vendors called out prices, a man played accordion, and somewhere a machine ground coffee beans. Luke steered Grandpa toward Mr. Taylor's stall, where Forrest was stacking tomatoes in an intricate pattern, each row balanced on the one below it.

"Grandpa, this is Forrest," Luke said. "And that's Emerson, the one waving."

Grandpa smiled and nodded, but when Forrest said, "Nice to meet you, sir, do you like tomatoes?" Grandpa answered, "Yes, it's a fine morning." Luke frowned. That wasn't an answer to the question. At home Grandpa never missed anything. He tested it, leaning close to Grandpa's ear and saying the same thing Forrest had said, slowly, and Grandpa answered right away, "Tomatoes? Sure, the red ones."

So Grandpa's ears worked. Something about the market was the problem. Luke watched and began to notice a pattern. When the accordion stopped between songs, Grandpa chatted easily with Mr. Taylor about the weather. When the music started up again, Grandpa nodded politely at things that weren't questions. The noise was doing something that quiet wasn't. That was it, Luke thought. For someone like Grandpa, following speech got harder when there was background noise, even for the same words that worked fine at the kitchen table.

"Emerson," Luke said, "the noise here is like the antagonist of every conversation." Emerson laughed and wrote that down in the little notebook she used to document stuff for the school paper, and then she had an idea. She flipped to a blank page and wrote GRANDPA? in big letters, then TOMATOES? and HOW MUCH?

Grandpa read the page and grinned. "A dollar fifty for the tomatoes," he said, pointing at Mr. Taylor's chalkboard sign, "and yes, I'd like some." Mr. Taylor bagged them while Forrest gave Luke a thumbs-up.

They found a bench behind the market where it was quiet, and Grandpa told the paperboy story all over again, this time to Forrest and Emerson, who had never heard it. When the accordion started up again in the distance, Grandpa just leaned closer to the kids and kept talking.

"Now that," he said, holding up a tomato, "is worth a dollar fifty."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: A battery turns stored chemical energy into electrical energy, and it goes flat when those chemicals are used up.
story:
Camille had built the circuit on Tuesday, and the bulb had glowed as soon as she closed the switch. Yesterday it worked. Today, in the back of the science room, she closed the switch and nothing happened. She flicked it three more times, faster each time.

"Maybe the switch is broken," said Dhruv, leaning over her table. "My dad says switches wear out."

Camille shook her head. "It worked yesterday. A switch doesn't wear out overnight." She unscrewed the bulb and held it up to the window. The filament inside looked whole, a thin silver thread, not snapped or blackened. She screwed it back in and closed the switch again. Still dark.

Ms. Francis walked past and set a small tray of fresh batteries on the counter, but she said nothing, which Camille took to mean: figure it out yourself. Camille remembered her grandfather telling her about the old radio on the farm, how the peasant who lived next door once walked ten kilometres to town just to buy new batteries, because the radio had gone silent in the middle of a storm. "No batteries, no radio," he had said. At the time Camille had thought batteries were like water pipes, something that carried power from somewhere far away. Now she wondered if that was wrong.

She took one wire off the switch and touched it straight to the bulb holder, bypassing the switch entirely. If the switch was the problem, the bulb should light. It stayed dark. So the switch was not it. That left the bulb, the wires, or the battery. The bulb looked fine. The wires were copper all the way along, and yesterday they had carried current just fine. She crossed the room, took a fresh battery from the tray, and clipped it into place. She closed the switch. The bulb lit, steady and yellow.

"It was the battery," she said. "The old one ran out."

Allegra frowned from the next table. "Ran out? Batteries don't have anything in them to run out of. They're just, like, blocks."

"They have chemicals in them," Camille said. "That's where the power sits, stored up. The battery turns that into electrical energy, and when the chemicals get used up, it's flat. Ours was flat." She turned the dead battery over in her hand. It weighed the same as the new one, which was strange, since it was empty.

Dhruv wrote FLAT BATTERY on a scrap of paper and taped it to the dead one. "For the evidence board," he said. "Ms. Francis says the circuit has to be fundamental to our project. We can't have it dying the night before the fair."

"Then we get a spare," Camille said, and took two more batteries from the tray.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Muffin tops turn golden brown in the oven because sugars and proteins react in the heat, a process called the Maillard reaction.
story:
Gabriel slid the recipe card across the steel counter and read it top to bottom twice. "Step one: preheat the oven to three seventy-five." He spun the dial, listened for the click and the low rumble of heat, and felt like he had launched a rocket. This was his first Saturday at the community kitchen, and Mr. Mori had promised that anyone who finished a full recipe alone would earn an apron with the kitchen's logo stitched on the pocket.

"Blueberry or plain?" asked Paige, who was already halfway through her own card at the next station.

"Blueberry. Obviously." Emanuel grabbed a mixing bowl for him before Gabriel could even ask. The kitchen smelled like cinnamon from the morning class, and sunlight warmed the flour bins along the wall.

Gabriel measured, cracked two eggs, and stirred until his arm ached. He spooned the batter into twelve cups, and that was when the trouble started. The recipe said bake for twenty minutes, but the tops were still pale and wet-looking at the halfway check. He crouched at the little oven window, watching through the opaque glass, and a worry crept in. If they never browned, they would look raw, and Mr. Mori might decide he hadn't really finished the recipe.

Then he noticed something. Paige's tray, already cooling on the rack, had turned a deep golden brown on top, but when she broke one open to taste, the inside was still pale and soft. Same batter color, same oven. So the browning wasn't the batter changing all the way through. Something was happening only where the heat touched the surface. He thought about toast, and how bread goes golden on the outside while the middle stays white, and he had an idea.

He knocked on Mr. Mori's office door. "Is there a name for when the outside browns but the inside stays pale? Like it's the sugars doing it?"

Mr. Mori grinned. "Sugars and proteins react in the heat. It's called the Maillard reaction."

"Maillard," Gabriel repeated, racing back to his oven. At twenty minutes he opened the door, and there they were: twelve domed tops, transformed from wet grey to glowing gold, steam curling up and the smell of blueberries filling the whole kitchen. He bit into one carefully, and the pale inside gave way soft and warm. Paige leaned over and stole the smallest one, and Emanuel was already reading the next recipe card, tapping the oatmeal muffins.

"Same time next week?" Emanuel said. Gabriel tied his new apron strings in a double knot and slid the card into his pocket.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe, so "a black cat" is "un gato negro."
story:
Carson stared at the card Ms. Baptiste had handed out and felt a wave of despair. On Friday, each student in Spanish class had to stand up and describe their family and pets in full sentences, and today was Wednesday. His sentences kept coming out wrong on the practice sheet, and he could not figure out why.

"Tengo un gato negro," said Trinity, reading off her paper in the library after school. She had a photo of her cat, Midnight, tucked under the book she was studying.

"That sounds backwards," Carson said. "You wrote the colors after the animal. Shouldn't it be negro gato?" He looked at his own sheet, where he had written "un perro marrón" and then scratched it out and written "un marrón perro" instead.

Trinity frowned at her paper. "I copied mine from the board. Ms. Baptiste wrote it that way."

Carson sat back and thought about it. Maybe there was a pattern he was missing. He flipped through the class workbook and found three more examples: "una casa grande," "un libro rojo," "una profesora alta." In every single one, the describing word came after the noun. He grabbed a pencil. "I think I've got it. Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe. So a black cat is un gato negro, not un negro gato."

"Then your dog is the brown one coming second too," Trinity said. "Un perro marrón was right the first time."

Carson erased his scratch-out and rewrote it. "We should verify it before Friday, though. Let's ask Ayesha. She spent a summer with her grandmother, and they only spoke Spanish at home."

They found Ayesha at the art table, painting a luminous yellow sun. Carson read his sentence aloud, and she nodded before he even finished. "That's how my abuela says it," she said. "Gato negro, casa grande. Always after."

Carson grinned and wrote four more sentences, each one with the describing word in the right place. When the bell rang, he slid the practice sheet into his folder and tapped the cover twice for luck.

"Ready for Friday?" Trinity asked, gathering her books.

"Almost," Carson said. "I just have to remember my dog's name in Spanish class. At home he only answers to Stinky."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
Nora slid into the seat behind Tim and leaned over the backrest, because the argument from lunch was still burning in her. "Jeter," Tim said, not even turning around. "Justice," Nora said. "I looked them up last night. Justice hit for a higher average than Jeter in 1995."

Allyson, sitting across the aisle, pulled out her phone. The bus rattled over the speed bump by the gym, and she steadied the screen with her sleeve so they could both see the numbers. "Here's 1996," she said. "Justice again. Higher average than Jeter both years."

"Ha," said Nora. But Tim jabbed a finger at a lower line on the screen, one she hadn't noticed. "Combined, though. Jeter's ahead." Nora grabbed the phone and scrolled back and forth, checking the two season lines against the combined one, certain one of them had read it wrong. She hadn't. Justice won in 1995, Justice won in 1996, and somehow Jeter won when the seasons were put together. It felt like a magic trick with no magician.

She sat back and tried to infer what was going on, since the reason wasn't visible anywhere on the screen. Maybe it was like when the morning announcements said the eighth grade averaged twenty points a game, and that single number flattened every blowout and every shutout into one tidy figure. The rankings on sports shows did the same thing, squeezing a whole season into one slot. "It's like the average isn't the whole story," she said slowly. "One number can hide stuff. There must be some other variable that changes when you add the years."

Tim turned around fully now, kneeling on his seat despite the driver's rule about knees on cushions. "So who's actually better?"

"I don't know," Nora admitted, and it felt strange and good to say it. Allyson held the phone flat between the three of them, screen catching the window light, so transparent with smudged fingerprints that she wiped it on her jacket first. "Let's check their whole careers," she said.

"Do it before my stop," Tim said. The bus swung around the corner toward Maple Street, and Nora pulled her lunch money out of her pocket to trade for Allyson's seat, the one with the working window latch, so they could see the screen the whole way.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks; the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck.
story:
Leo set the two jars on the garden wall where he could watch them from the kitchen window. One held broth he had boiled on the stove; the other held broth from the same pot, but sealed while it was still steaming. For the science fair he needed an answer, and he had a hypothesis, which Sadie had told him meant a guess you could actually test. His guess was this: it was not the broth that went bad on its own, but something floating into it from the air. Three days later, the open jar had turned cloudy and smelled like old shoes. The sealed one stayed clear. He almost cheered, until Stevie leaned over the wall and squinted at the clean jar.

"That doesn't prove anything," Stevie said. "Maybe sealing it just kept it fresh, like cling wrap on a sandwich. Maybe air itself spoils food, not stuff in the air." Leo felt a drop of dread, cold and sudden, because Stevie might be right. A hypothesis was supposed to survive being attacked, and his had a hole in it.

He went to Mr. Korhonen next door, who kept beakers and glass tubes in his garden shed and let Leo borrow what he called "competent equipment, not toy store junk." Leo heated a glass tube with the little burner and bent it, twice, into a long S-shaped neck, then fitted it to a flask of broth and boiled the whole thing. The flask was open at the end. Air could get in freely, so if plain air were the culprit, this broth should spoil too. He set the flask on the wall beside a second one with a straight open neck and checked it every morning, hating how slowly the days moved.

On the fifth day the straight-necked broth had gone cloudy. The S-necked broth sat clear as rainwater. Leo flipped through the book Mr. Korhonen had handed him, and there it was: Louis Pasteur had done exactly this, boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck.

"Microbes," Leo read aloud, then said it again, grinning. "Stevie! Stevie, get over here and look at my flask."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: In the Three Sisters method used by many Indigenous peoples of the Americas, corn supports climbing beans, and squash leaves shade the soil against weeds.
story:
Savannah knelt on her apartment balcony with three buckets in front of her, a bag of soil, and a packet of corn seeds. Downstairs, in the community garden behind the building, Ms. Campbell-Brown's plot was planted in strange little hills, three different plants crowded together, and Savannah wanted to know why. Her own beans had flopped over last summer, snapping where the stems bent, and she refused to let that happen again. This year she had a theory: the garden plot held the answer, if she could read it.

Junior leaned over the railing from the next balcony, because what he wanted was to be the first to eat whatever grew. "That's not a garden, that's a mess," he said, pointing at the buckets. "Corn there, beans there, squash over there."

"Ms. Campbell-Brown didn't plant hers that way," Savannah said. She counted on her fingers. "Corn in a mound, beans right beside it, squash all around the bottom. Every hill, same pattern. That's not a mess, that's a plan." She dragged her fingertips through the cool soil and smelled that dark, rain-like smell of it. "Beans climb. What if they climb the corn?"

Junior made a face, so she kept her voice neutral and said, "We'll see. You can refute me at dinner." She pushed the corn seeds into the middle bucket, dropped bean seeds beside them, and tucked two squash seeds in the outside ring, where their wide, prickly-edged leaves would sprawl. The last squash seed had a hairline fracture running down its pale coat, and she planted it anyway, curious whether it would still sprout.

For two weeks she measured everything. The corn rose first, straight and stiff. Then the beans appeared, and by the time they had two leaves each, they were leaning, curling, reaching until the tips of them found the corn stalks and gripped. "Look," Savannah whispered one evening, holding her ruler against the stalk while the vine wound another slow loop around it. The squash came last, flat leaves spreading until they shaded the whole surface of the bucket.

Junior arrived that morning with a fork in his back pocket. He crouched, inspected the shaded soil, and poked at it. "No weeds," he said, sounding almost disappointed. "There were weeds all over my mom's tomatoes."

"That's the leaves," Savannah said. She lifted one gently to show him the dark, damp ground underneath. "Ms. Campbell-Brown called it the Three Sisters. Corn holds the beans up, squash keeps the weeds down." She picked the first tiny bean pod, warm from the sun, and dropped it into Junior's hand.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect.
story:
Gabriel spread seven paper airplanes across the kitchen table like a fleet of very confused birds. His science fair project was due Friday, and something was wrong with it, had been wrong since Tuesday. He had changed the wing shape on each plane, which was the point, but he had also switched from heavy paper to thin paper halfway through, because he ran out of the heavy kind. Now his distance chart looked like it had been drawn by a sneezing seismograph. Kevin leaned over the papers, chewing a granola bar. "So just say the thin-paper ones went farther," he said. "Problem solved. Snack?"

Gabriel shook his head. He remembered Mr. Moose, the neighbour who had judged the fair last year, tapping Gabriel's volcano poster with one finger and saying, "Nice lava. What exactly did you change?" Gabriel hadn't had an answer then, and the irony of building a second project with the same hole was not lost on him. He picked up two planes. "Listen. The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose. The dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect." Kevin blinked. "You memorized that?" "I wrote it on my hand," Gabriel admitted, showing a smudged palm. "The independent variable is supposed to be wing shape only. I changed the paper too, so the whole thing is a mess." Kevin looked at the chart, then at the planes, then at the last apple in the bowl, clearly prioritizing. "So fly them again, all on the same paper, legitimate test, and I get the apple."

They refolded the fleet from one stack of identical paper and threw each plane three times down the hallway, marking distances in pencil on the baseboard. Gabriel devised a simple rotating order, throwing one plane of each shape per round so his arm getting tired wouldn't sneak in as a third variable. The surprise came at the end. The plane with the plain rectangular wings, the boring one, the one Gabriel had folded first as a "control before he knew the word," sailed past every dart and glider and smacked the bathroom door. Kevin saluted it. Gabriel stared at his chart, where a clear pattern now climbed across the columns. He picked up the boring plane gently, like something that had earned respect. "Friday," he told it, "you're going first."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words, 'Veni, vidi, vici': I came, I saw, I conquered.
story:
Hunter stood at the free-throw line in the empty gym, holding his note cards like they might bite him. Mr. Chanthavong had said every seventh grader would give a two-minute speech on Friday, and Hunter's cards numbered seven points, which felt proportional to how nervous he was. The problem was that his practice runs kept hitting three minutes, then four, and the whole thing collapsed into a pile of facts about volcanoes.

Frank sat on the bleachers tossing a volleyball at the wall. "You're going to put the whole gym to sleep."

"I just need to talk faster," Hunter said.

Thiago jogged over from the equipment room with a badminton racket balanced on his chin, because that was Thiago. "Talking faster is not the answer. Remember when I did my book report on Julius Caesar? He reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words. Veni, vidi, vici."

"What's that mean?" Frank asked.

"I came, I saw, I conquered," Thiago said, and the racket slid off his chin and clattered on the floor.

Hunter looked at his seven cards. Three words, three points. Maybe that was the hidden rule, the reason speeches felt solid instead of mushy. He decided to test it right there. He dealt his cards like a magician, keeping only the three best ones, and pushed the rest under the bleachers.

"Ladies and gentlemen," he began, imagining the gym packed and the basketball hoop glowing like a golden gate, "did you know a volcano in Italy once provoked a war? No? Then listen." He gave his three points, slow and clear, and when he said his last line the sound of his voice bounced off the far wall and came back to him like applause.

Hunter clicked the stopwatch. One minute, fifty-two seconds.

"Again," he said, shuffling his cards like a card sharp in a movie. "This time you two heckle me."

activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
knowledge_domain: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
fact: Runners learning a three-step rhythm often practice with hurdles set lower and closer together than race spacing, then move them apart as they get faster.
story:
Ella stood at the far end of the baseball diamond, where Ms. Grewal had set a row of low hurdles along the outfield grass. The outfield fence smelled like hot dust, and someone's radio played behind the concession stand. Lara and Maddison were already jogging back from the far end, their feet slapping the hard dirt between second base and the wall.

"Three steps between each one," Maddison called. "One, two, three, hop."

Eella tried it. She cleared the first hurdle, counted one-two-three, and then had to stretch and lurch for the second, catching it with her trailing knee. The hurdle tipped and clattered onto the grass. She tried again and did the same thing. On the third try she took four steps and still barely reached it.

She watched Lara go instead. Lara popped over the first hurdle and arrived at the second with room to spare. Ella stood behind her and counted, then walked the gap between hurdles with her own feet. Lara covered more ground in each step than she did. That was the hidden problem, Ella realized. It was not the jumping. It was the distance in between, which her legs could not cross in only three steps.

She thought about how the hurdles were spaced here, wider than what felt right for her stride, like race spacing. She went to Ms. Grewal by the backstop. "Can we move them lower and closer together?" Ella asked. "Just for practice. Then move them apart as I get faster."

"That's exactly how it works," Ms. Grewal said. "Gradual is the whole point. Prioritize the rhythm first, speed later."

Ella and Maddison slid the hurdles together until the gaps felt possible. Ella ran, and this time her feet found one-two-three, hop, one-two-three, hop, all the way down the row without touching a single bar. Afterward she sat on the bench by the fence, drinking a lemonade she had bought, since she was the team's most devoted consumer of concession stand drinks. Lara came over and bumped her shoulder.

"Same time tomorrow?" Lara said.

"Bring your legs," said Ella. "Mine are still figuring it out."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.
story:
