The regional spelling bee had been moved to the public library at the last minute, which meant Amelia was competing between the biography shelves and a poster of a wetland ecosystem, complete with a cartoon heron. She had studied word lists for months, but she still felt a little reckless skipping her Saturday cartoons for this.

"Your word is 'seismometer,'" said the judge, a librarian with reading glasses parked low on her nose.

Amelia's mind went blank. She knew "meter" had to mean measure, but the middle was a swamp. Juliet, sitting in the front row with their whole class, gave her a thumbs up so enthusiastic it nearly knocked Prince's glasses off.

Then Amelia remembered something her older cousin had grumbled about after watching the Scripps National Spelling Bee on TV. "Wait," she said. "Can I ask for the definition?"

"You may," the librarian said. "An instrument that measures earthquakes."

"And the part of speech?"

"Noun."

"Could I have the language of origin?"

"Greek."

Something clicked. Earthquakes, Greek, "seis-" like the word on the earthquake poster in her science classroom, the one Prince had once tried to oppose by arguing that volcanoes were more interesting. S-E-I-S-M-O-M-E-T-E-R. She could see the whole thing now, letter by letter.

"Seismometer. S-E-I-S-M-O-M-E-T-E-R. Seismometer."

"Correct."

Juliet clapped so loudly that the librarian gave her the look usually reserved for people who dog-ear books. During the break, Prince slid over with a granola bar. "I thought you were going to ask for a sentence too," he said. "You know, like a word in a sentence?"

"I almost did," Amelia said, tearing the wrapper. "But once I heard Greek, I didn't need it. I'm saving that one for the final round." She pointed her granola bar at the heron poster. "Watch out. Next word might be about that ecosystem."

The librarian's voice came over the speaker: "Finalists, take your places, please."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
story:
David's violin note kept sagging, and he could not figure out why. Every time he lifted his bow in Ms. Nkosi's music classroom, the A string sounded fine for a few seconds and then drooped, like it was tired of being played. Brogan, two seats over, had already started calling it "the sad whale," and the others had laughed along, though Kash at least had the decency to keep his face neutral.

David tried playing harder, then softer, then standing closer to the window, as if the sound needed better air. Nothing helped. At home he sat with the violin on his lap and plucked the string with one finger, watching it shiver. He pressed the string down against the fingerboard with his other hand and plucked again. Lower. He slid his finger up toward the bridge. Higher. The string was getting shorter, he thought, so there was less of it to move. Maybe less moving meant slower moving, and slower meant lower. Faster would mean higher. It was a guess about something invisible, and the only way to check it was to make the string move faster or slower on purpose.

The next morning he got to class early and borrowed the small tuning fork from Ms. Nkosi's shelf. He struck it, held it near the string, and listened. Then he turned the fine tuner a tiny bit and struck it again. Tighter, the note crept up. He loosened it, and the note slid back down, sinking like a paper boat taking on water. So a string that was tighter vibrated faster, and faster vibration made the pitch higher. Looser meant slower, and lower. He wrote it in his notebook in careful letters: faster vibration, higher note. Slower vibration, lower note.

That gave him a new dilemma. His own string drooped while he played, which meant it was going slower and slower, which meant it was slipping loose. The problem wasn't him. It was the peg. After school he asked Ms. Nkosi if he could look at it, and together they pushed the peg firmly into its hole while he tuned. The string held. He drew the bow across it and the A came out round and steady, no sad whale anywhere.

Brogan walked past and said, "Let's hear the whale."

David set the bow down and lifted the violin. "Extinct," he said, and played the note twice, clean as a bell.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Robert Paine introduced the term 'keystone species' in 1969 for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest.
story:
Leo sat cross-legged on the flat rock at the edge of Miller Pond, his notebook open to a page with a wobbly arrow chain: sun, then algae, then water bugs, then minnows, then three big bass he'd drawn with jagged teeth because it looked fiercer that way. His assignment was to explain what happened if one link vanished, and he had no idea. Aryan crouched beside him, poking a stick at the green scum near the shore. "That pond behind the school doesn't have any of this stuff," Aryan said. "The water's clear and there's hardly anything swimming in it." Leo stopped drawing. The two ponds were only a mile apart. Same sun, same bugs, same kind of minnows. The one difference he knew for sure was that nobody had ever caught a bass in the school pond.

"That's my test," Leo said. "Fewer predators, different pond." The next Saturday he and Charlie dragged two nets through both ponds, counting everything they caught, and Charlie wrote the numbers down with vigorous scribbles because his pencil kept breaking. In Miller Pond they netted minnows by the dozen and scopped up thick green strands of algae. In the school pond they found minnows, minnows, and more minnows, swarming everywhere, but the water was oddly bare and the rocks were picked clean. Only three bass lived in Miller Pond, Charlie pointed out, out of hundreds of fish, yet those three seemed to matter more than all the minnows put together.

Leo took his two drawings to Ms. Watanabe, who kept a shelf of science books beside her garden tools. He showed her the chain and the counts, and she handed him a worn paperback and let him read at her kitchen table while the cat accompanied her from chair to sink and back. One line stopped him cold. In 1969, Robert Paine had watched a shoreline change completely after he removed a single predator, and he called that kind of animal a keystone species. Leo read the words twice. Keystone. Like the stone in an arch.

On Monday he balanced wooden blocks on the porch railing and built an arch with Aryan and Charlie watching. He set the last block at the top center, then reached in and pulled it out. The whole arch thudded down around his wrist. "Keystone species," Leo said, holding up the block. "Three skinny bass. Take them away and the entire pond belongs to the minnows." Charlie was already stacking the blocks again. "Build it taller this time," he said, "and pull out one of the side ones too, so we can see it not fall."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Scooping flour straight from the bag with a measuring cup packs it down and can add noticeably more flour than spooning it in and levelling it off.
story:
At six in the morning the farmers' market pavilion smelled like hay and cinnamon, and Taylor was already perspiring over a folding table that Mr. Iyer had lent her for the day. She and Kayleigh had signed up to sell muffins at the school's market stall, and the deal was that everything had to be on the table by nine, when the first customers wandered in with their canvas bags. The motivation was simple: the booth fee had already been paid, and Taylor's mother had said, twice, that she was not going to eat a single rescue muffin.

Taylor's batch came out of Mr. Iyer's big oven looking the way the recipe photo looked, round and golden. Kayleigh's batch, from the exact same recipe, came out squat and pale and heavy as hockey pucks. "We used the same recipe," Kayleigh said, poking one with a fork. "We even measured everything. Same recipe." Taylor turned a muffin over and thought about the one part nobody could see, the part hidden inside the batter before it ever reached the oven.

She watched Kayleigh make the next test batch, and there it was: Kayleigh dunked her measuring cup straight into the flour bag and dug, packing the cup full, then swept it level with a knife. Taylor, for her own batch, had spooned flour gently into the cup and then levelled it off, so hers held less. Taylor weighed both cups on Mr. Iyer's cheese scale, and Kayleigh's was heavier by a margin that made her groan. "So mine has extra flour the whole time," Kayleigh said. "That's why they're dry little bricks."

They remade Kayleigh's batch the spoon-and-level way, slid the pans in, and watched the clock crawl toward nine. At four minutes to, Mr. Iyer strolled past the stall, sniffed, and raised an eyebrow at the two matching rows of muffins. "Dare I ask which ones are whose?" Taylor wrapped the first sample in a napkin and held it out to him. "Guess," she said.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
story:
Nicolas set his fork down and stared at his plate. His dad had asked how school was, and Nicolas had said "fine," which was true in the way that a flat tire means the car still rolls.

"You're pushing peas around like they hinder your dinner," his dad said, trying for a joke. It didn't land.

That morning, Nicolas had posted a photo of himself in his gym shorts with a mustard stain shaped like a duck. He'd meant to send it just to Roger, but he'd posted it publicly by accident. Ten minutes later he'd deleted it, and he'd felt the relief wash over him, like closing a door on something embarrassing. Then, at lunch, Cecilia had slid her phone across the table and shown him the group chat. The duck stain was there. Roger had screenshotted it before Nicolas deleted the post.

"The whole basketball team has it," Roger had admitted, looking sorry. "I only sent it to one person. I didn't think it would spread like a plague."

Nicolas had spent the afternoon working it out. He couldn't see where the photo was now, the way you can't see where a cold goes when it travels through a classroom. But he could test one thing. He asked Roger to send it to exactly one friend, then waited. By last period, three kids Nicolas had never met were quacking at him in the hallway. So deleting the post had only taken it off his own page. Every copy that anyone had already saved, they still had.

"Is it the photo?" his dad asked now. "The one with the duck?"

Nicolas looked up, startled. His dad tapped his own phone. "Ms. Santos sent me a message. She's the coach's neighbor, apparently, and she saw it on her son's phone this afternoon. She wanted to warn you before it reached more parents."

So it had jumped even that fence. Nicolas explained what he'd figured out, that deleting wasn't the equivalent of taking a picture off the wall, because people could have copies they'd made before it vanished. His dad listened without interrupting, which was its own kind of help.

"Okay," his dad said. "So what's your plan?"

Nicolas picked his fork back up. He'd already texted Roger and Cecilia and asked them, one at a time, to delete their copies and ask whoever they'd sent it to do the same. It was like pulling weeds from the roots instead of snapping off the tops. By tomorrow the copies would be fewer. And he'd already decided his next embarrassing photo would go to Roger and Roger only.

"Copies first, then captions," he said. "Roger's writing an apology message tonight. He says the duck deserves a better debut."

His dad laughed, and Nicolas took the first real bite of his dinner.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
The garage sale at Mr. Hoang's house had three folding tables, and Hannah had exactly four dollars and one nickel. She wanted the old poetry book with the green cover, the one with a stanza about rivers circled in pencil, but Dalia wanted it too, and so did a boy who kept picking it up and putting it down. On the next table sat a whole cardboard box of water bottles, fifty cents each, and nobody was buying them at all. "Why is the box of water so cheap and the little glass stone so expensive?" Hannah asked Mr. Hoang, pointing at a tiny gem marked fifteen dollars. "Because five people have asked me about the stone since eight o'clock," he said, "and nobody has asked about the water."

Hannah thought about that while she waited for Dalia to make up her mind. She was starting to perspire in the heat, and she noticed that people kept walking past the water to look at the stone, the book, and a radio that had only one left of its kind. Then two girls came by and asked Mr. Hoang whether the water was safe, because someone had told them the old bottles could be toxic. He said no, it was fine, but they still didn't buy any, because there was a whole box of it and a store on the corner.

"You know what my mom told me last night?" Dalia said, fanning herself with her hand. "There was a guy named Adam Smith, and in 1776 he published a book, 'The Wealth of Nations', and he said nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." Hannah stared at her. That was exactly the box of water and the tiny stone. "So it isn't about how useful something is," she said slowly. "It's about how many people want it and how few there are."

She had an idea, and she tested it right there. "Mr. Hoang," she said, "there's only one green poetry book, and three of us want it. Would you take my four dollars and nickel if I promise to write my favorite stanza on a card for Dalia so she gets part of it too?" The boy with the wandering hands had wandered off toward the radio, which left two buyers instead of three. Mr. Hoang looked at the box of untouched water, then at the crowd around his rare things, and grinned. "Sold," he said, and wrapped the book in yesterday's newspaper.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
story:
Emilia pulled her synthetic rain jacket out of her backpack at Gate C14 and shoved it back down again, because it was snowing in her hometown and twenty-five degrees where she was going. Beside her, Oceane was reading the travel brochure for the fourth time. Oceane's family and Emilia's were flying together to the coast for a whole week.

"There's a beach right behind the hotel," Oceane said. "It says swimming is allowed but there's a lifeguard sign at the entrance."

"What kind of sign?" Emilia asked. She liked to classify warnings into the ones you could ignore and the ones you couldn't, like the difference between "slippery floor" and "do not climb."

Oceane turned the page. "It says rip currents. My mom told me about those, the water pulls you out away from the beach, and people panic and try to swim straight back in and get too tired."

Emilia thought about that. A current pulling out had to be like a river, and rivers weren't wide everywhere. If the pull was narrow, then swimming sideways, along the beach instead of against the pull, might carry you out of it. She had never seen a rip current, but she could picture the shape.

"Watch," she said, and dug a shoelace out of her backpack pocket. At the window she laid it on the sill, laid her finger on the middle of it, and dragged her finger straight back toward the window frame. Then she slid her finger sideways instead, off the shoelace entirely, and touched the bare sill. "That's the beach, that way. If the current is only as wide as the shoelace, you get out of it sideways."

"So you swim parallel to the beach," Oceane said slowly, "not straight against it."

"That's my guess anyway."

"You sound like Mr. Grant in science class."

A man two seats over looked up from his newspaper. "Lifeguard, fourteen years," he said. "That's exactly what we teach. Swim along the beach till you're out of the narrow thing, then come in. Most kids don't figure that out on their own."

Emilia felt her face go warm. She folded the shoelace and put it back in her pocket, and when the boarding call came she stood up, smoothing her peasant blouse, and said, "Race you to the scanner."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Blue-enriched light from phone screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening.
story:
On Tuesday morning Ms. Goh set a small box on Jeremy's desk, and by lunch he had learned that his new phone could do eleven things his brain wanted to do all at once. His mother had written a note that morning and tucked it into his backpack, and he read it again during silent reading while the phone sat in his pocket like a warm coin. "This phone will accompany you to school and back," the note said, "but not into your bed at night. Signed, a person who once fell asleep at her own desk for eleven years straight." Jeremy folded the note into his pocket next to the warm coin, which buzzed twice before the bell.

For four nights he scrolled in bed anyway, flashlight games and video after video, because everyone in his class did it and the screen looked best in the dark. For four mornings he dragged himself into Ms. Goh's classroom like a boy wading through syrup. Natasha noticed on Friday. "You look like Kaysen's fish when the filter broke," she whispered, and Kaysen said, "That fish looked bad, though, so fair."

Jeremy decided to test it like a science experiment, since Ms. Goh was always saying a good critique of your own idea beats a perfect guess. Friday night he left the phone charging in the kitchen and lay in bed with nothing but the ceiling. He was asleep before he finished counting the third crack. Saturday night he scrolled in bed until eleven and stared at the ceiling until nearly midnight, wide awake, eyes burning. Sunday he left the phone in the kitchen again and dropped off fast. Same room, same pillow, same ceiling. The only thing that changed was the screen.

On Monday he found Natasha by the cubbies. "I think the light from the screen does something," he said. "Blue-ish light. When I scroll in bed, my body won't let me get sleepy, and when I don't, it does. I looked it up this weekend on the kitchen computer, not in bed."

"Melatonin," Natasha said. "That's what the website called it. The hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening. Kaysen read the same page because his brother plays games under the covers till one in the morning and is basically a zombie at breakfast."

Jeremy considered this. "So the screen delays the melatonin, or slows it, and then you just lie there." He held up the phone. "Which means this thing is a sleep thief that fits in a sock. It's ironic, honestly. The stuff I scroll to fall asleep is the stuff keeping me up."

Natasha peered at the phone in his hand. "Is that a flashlight app?"

"It's a blue-light experiment," Jeremy said, and he turned the screen face-down on the desk.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: A dress rehearsal is a full run-through shortly before the first performance, done as if it were the real show, usually in costume.
story:
The note was waiting in Penelope's trumpet case when she opened it after lunch. In Kristian's scrawly handwriting it said, "Practice was wrong today. You sounded like you were whispering the whole song. What happened? Meet me in the gym before rehearsal." She folded the note into her pocket and thought about the morning, when she had sung so quietly that even she could barely hear herself.

At the gym, Ms. Watanabe was hanging the costumes on a rolling rack. "Tomorrow's concert, so today we do the dress rehearsal," she said. "A full run-through, as if it were the real show, and you perform in costume." Penelope had never worn her costume before. It was a silver tunic with a stiff, high collar, and when she pulled it on, it squeezed her ribs like a fist. She tried to take the deep breath she needed for the long note in the second verse, and nothing came. That was the answer to Kristian's note. She hadn't been whispering on purpose. Her old practice shirt had been fine, so her quiet singing in class had seemed like nerves, but now, in costume, she felt the real cause.

She remembered the fall talent show, when Emmitt had frozen halfway through his magic act and stood there red-faced until Ms. Watanabe finally clapped. Afterward he told her the stage lights had been so hot he couldn't think. She didn't want tomorrow to go that way.

Penelope tried an experiment. She unfastened the top hook of the collar, pulled the tunic down a centimeter at the shoulders, and breathed in. Air rushed in all the way down to the bottom of her lungs. "Ms. Watanabe," she called, "could I sing the run-through like this, with one hook open?" Ms. Watanabe walked over, tugged the fabric, and nodded. "Better loose than silent."

Kristian started the piano intro. Penelope filled her lungs, and the long note in the second verse came out strong and clear, bouncing off the gym ceiling.

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: A short sentence placed after several long ones stands out, so writers often use one for the moment they most want the reader to notice.
story:
Joshua had written the same sentence four times, and Mr. Gagnon still wanted more. "Cut 'really big' and 'very dark' and 'kind of scary,'" he had written at the top of Joshua's draft in red pen. "Then look at your sentence lengths." The story was due on Friday, and Joshua wanted it to be the one Mr. Gagnon read out loud to the class, because last time he had picked Katherine's paper, and hers was about a horse.

At lunch, Joshua spread his draft on the table next to his milk. Lucas leaned over from the next seat. "You wrote 'very very quiet' twice," Lucas said. "That's not even an adjective anymore, that's a cry for help." Joshua crossed out "very very quiet," and just "quiet" stayed, which was strange because quiet seemed louder now, like the word had room to breathe.

Then he counted the sentences in his cave scene. Four of them ran long, one after another, all with commas, dragging their feet down the page. The fifth was "He heard a drip." It sat there alone, and when Joshua read the page again, that little sentence jumped off the line at him. He tried an experiment. He moved "He heard a drip" to the middle of the paragraph, and it disappeared, like a minnow in a school of minnows. He moved it back to the end. There it was again.

"Listen to this," Joshua said, and read the cave scene aloud to Lucas. Lucas stopped chewing his sandwich at "He heard a drip," then admitted that was creepy, which for Lucas was a big concession.

On Friday, Mr. Gagnon read Joshua's paper to the class. He read slowly through the long sentences, and then he stopped. "He heard a drip."

The room went silent. Katherine, who thought nothing could beat her horse story, raised her hand and said, "Okay, that part got me."

"Now I just have to convert my dragon story," Lucas whispered across the aisle. "My dragon is imminent, and currently he is very very huge."
